t: Find the Level of Tree with Minimum Sum
o: We must compute the sum of node values at every level of a binary tree and return the smallest level index (1-based) achieving the minimum sum; ties go to the lowest level. In example 1, level sums lead to level 2 being minimal. Constraints allow up to 1e5 nodes, so we need an O(n) traversal — BFS or DFS both work. Values fit easily in 64-bit sums.
k: A level-order traversal naturally groups nodes by depth.
Any O(n) tree traversal suffices; recursion depth can hit 1e5, so iterative BFS is safer in some languages.

a.i: Process the tree level by level with a queue; for each level, sum the values of all nodes currently in the queue, track the minimum, then enqueue children.
s: Initialize a queue with the root, best sum = infinity, answer level = 1.
While the queue is non-empty, sum all nodes currently in it (one level).
If this sum is smaller than the best, record the level and sum.
Enqueue all non-null children; increment the level.
a.t: O(n) — every node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once
a.sp: O(w) — queue holds at most one level (tree width, up to O(n))

a.i: Recursively walk the tree carrying the depth; accumulate values into an array indexed by depth, then pick the first index holding the minimum.
s: Maintain a list `sums` where sums[d] is the total at depth d.
DFS: extend the list when a new depth is reached, add the node value.
Recurse on both children with depth+1.
Return (index of min in sums) + 1; index() returns the first occurrence, handling ties.
a.sp: O(h) recursion stack plus O(depth) sums array

w: BFS is the natural interview answer and avoids deep recursion on skewed trees (1e5 nodes could overflow a recursive stack in Python). Watch for 64-bit sums (values up to 1e9 with 1e5 nodes). Tie-breaking is automatic since we only update on strictly smaller sums / use first-minimum index. Follow-ups: maximum level, weighted levels, or doing it on an N-ary tree — all trivial variations of the same traversal.
